title: Luther's morning blessing
hookLine: from the Small Catechism: I thank you, my heavenly Father, through Jesus Christ, that you have kept me this night
tomorrow: how can you be nobody's servant and everybody's?

cards: The alarm goes off, and a thumb is on the phone before both eyes are open: the news, the messages, whatever went wrong overnight. Martin Luther had a different first move in mind.
In his Small Catechism, a short book for teaching the faith at home, he writes out what to do on getting out of bed. And before he asks anything for the day, he says thank you for the night.

teach.b: First, Luther says, make the sign of the holy cross and say: in the name of God the Father, Son and Holy Ghost. Amen.
Then, kneeling or standing, say the Creed and the Lord's Prayer. And if you like, he adds, say this little prayer.
It opens with thanks to the heavenly Father, through Jesus Christ his dear Son, for keeping you this night from all harm and danger.
Only then does it ask: keep me this day too, from sin and every evil, so that all I do and my whole life may please you.
It hands everything over, body and soul and all things, into God's hands, and asks that God's holy angel stay near.
Then the catechism says: go to your work joyfully, perhaps singing a hymn. Two surprises worth passing on. A reformer starts the day with the sign of the cross.
And thanks comes before the to-do list.

Sleep is a small helplessness: for hours you guarded nothing, and you woke up anyway. A psalm says it too: "I laid me down and slept; I awaked; for the LORD sustained me." Luther simply makes that the first thing said.

how: Some Lutheran households and others pray Luther's morning and evening prayers from the Small Catechism, often with the sign of the cross, the Creed and the Lord's Prayer.

games.q: your dad comes home at dawn after a night shift fighting a fire, wiped out. you're making coffee. what fits Luther's order for a morning?
o: start with thanks that he's home safe, then ask about the day.
ask him straight away what needs doing today.
skip it; mornings after night shifts don't really count.
games.why: Luther's morning blessing thanks God for keeping us this night before it asks anything for the day.

practice: Count back through last night on your fingers: the bed, the dark hours, the waking, the first breath of the day. Each one came while you guarded nothing. If you pray, you can give thanks for each, the way Luther's prayer begins.

wordCard.voice: Luther's morning blessing. The short prayer in his Small Catechism that thanks God for the night before asking anything for the day.

carryVoice: Carry this: kept this night, and the thanks comes before the day's first ask. Until tomorrow.
